opening.text: Imagine you are hiking a steep mountain trail for the first time. The path forks. Rocks are loose. Fog hangs over the ridge. Then you meet a guide who has climbed this mountain many times. He says, “Stay close. Step where I step.”
You do not need to see the whole route. You only need to see him, and take the next step.
That is what it means to follow Jesus Christ. I would like to talk about that today.

mainMessage.text: The Savior invites every one of us to follow Him. He is not asking us to admire Him from a distance. He is asking us to walk with Him, to learn from Him, and to become more like Him. It takes daily effort. It will cost us something. But He goes before us, and He never leaves us on the trail alone.

blocks.text: He invites us, one by one.

When Jesus called His disciples, He often used just two words. “Follow me.” He said it to Philip. He said it to fishermen. He says it to us. The invitation is personal. He knows each of His sheep, and they know His voice.
The day following Jesus would go forth into Galilee, and findeth Philip, and saith unto him, Follow me.
My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me: And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.
President Ezra Taft Benson, then President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, said this in his talk “Born of God” from the October 1985 general conference.
When you choose to follow Christ, you choose to be changed. . . . Men \[and women\] changed for Christ will be captained by Christ. . . . Their will is swallowed up in His will.
Following Him is a choice. And it changes us.
He showed us the way.
A good guide does not only point. He walks the trail first. The Savior did the same. He served the poor. He forgave sinners. He prayed to His Father. He told His disciples to do as He had done.
For I have given you an example, that ye should do as I have done to you.

Verily, verily, I say unto you, this is my gospel; and ye know the things that ye must do in my church; for the works which ye have seen me do that shall ye also do; for that which ye have seen me do even that shall ye do;
President Ezra Taft Benson said this in his article “Jesus Christ—Gifts and Expectations” in the December 1988 Ensign. It is a magazine article, not a conference talk.

That man is greatest and most blessed and joyful whose life most closely approaches the pattern of the Christ. This has nothing to do with earthly wealth, power, or prestige. The only true test of greatness, blessedness, joyfulness is how close a life can come to being like the Master, Jesus Christ. He is the right way, the full truth, and the abundant life.
So the question is simple. What would He do here? Then we try to do it.
Following Him costs something.

A mountain climber leaves some things behind. The pack is lighter. The path is steeper. The Savior was honest about this. He said that following Him means denying ourselves and taking up our cross every day. That does not mean misery. It means we choose His way over our own, again and again.

And he said to them all, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me. For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: but whosoever will lose his life for my sake, the same shall save it.
Elder Richard G. Scott of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “Trust in the Lord” from the October 1995 general conference.

This life is an experience in profound trust—trust in Jesus Christ. . . . To trust means to obey willingly without knowing the end from the beginning (see Prov. 3:5–7). To produce fruit, your trust in the Lord must be more powerful and enduring than your confidence in your own personal feelings and experience.
We may not see the whole route. We trust the one who does.
We keep following when it is hard.

The fog rolls in. The legs get tired. Some people turn back. That happened to the Savior too. After a hard teaching, many of His disciples walked away. Jesus asked the Twelve if they would go too. Peter’s answer is one of the best answers in all of scripture.

From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him. Then said Jesus unto the twelve, Will ye also go away? Then Simon Peter answered him, Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life. And we believe and are sure that thou art that Christ, the Son of the living God.
Elder Robert D. Hales of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “Christian Courage: The Price of Discipleship” from the October 2008 general conference.
Through the years we learn that challenges to our faith are not new, and they aren’t likely to disappear soon. But true disciples of Christ see opportunity in the midst of opposition.
“To whom shall we go?” When doubts come, that is a good question to ask.
We grow as we go.

No one reaches the summit in an hour. We climb a little each day. Nephi taught that getting on the path is only the start. We press forward, and we keep feasting on the word of Christ. The goal is to become like Him.

And now, my beloved brethren, after ye have gotten into this strait and narrow path, I would ask if all is done? Behold, I say unto you, Nay; for ye have not come thus far save it were by the word of Christ with unshaken faith in him, relying wholly upon the merits of him who is mighty to save. Wherefore, ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men. Wherefore, if ye shall press forward, feasting upon the word of Christ, and endure to the end, behold, thus saith the Father: Ye shall have eternal life.

And know ye that ye shall be judges of this people, according to the judgment which I shall give unto you, which shall be just. Therefore, what manner of men ought ye to be? Verily I say unto you, even as I am.
Elder D. Todd Christofferson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles wrote this in his article “To Always Remember Him” in the April 2011 Ensign. It is a magazine article, not a conference talk.

. . . I can attest that over time our desire and capacity to always remember and follow the Savior will grow. We should patiently work toward that end and pray always for the discernment and divine help we need.
We do not have to be there yet. We only have to keep going.
He goes before us.

The best part of the guide story is this. The guide does not stand at the top and shout directions. He walks ahead, and he stays close. The Lord has promised the same. He goes before our face. He is on our right hand and our left. He lifts us when we stumble.

And whoso receiveth you, there I will be also, for I will go before your face. I will be on your right hand and on your left, and my Spirit shall be in your hearts, and mine angels round about you, to bear you up.
Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness.
Elder Jeffrey R. Holland of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “Tomorrow the Lord Will Do Wonders among You” from the April 2016 general conference.

The Lord blesses those who want to improve, who accept the need for commandments and try to keep them, who cherish Christlike virtues and strive to the best of their ability to acquire them. If you stumble in that pursuit, so does everyone; the Savior is there to help you keep going. . . . Soon enough you will have the success you seek.
Stumbling is not the end. He is right there.

story.title: Peter walks toward Jesus on the water

blocks.text: The disciples were in a boat in a storm. Jesus came to them, walking on the sea. Peter wanted to go to Him.

And Peter answered him and said, Lord, if it be thou, bid me come unto thee on the water. And he said, Come. And when Peter was come down out of the ship, he walked on the water, to go to Jesus. But when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me. And immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him, and said unto him, O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?

Peter stepped out of the boat. That took faith. When he looked at the wind instead of the Lord, he began to sink. But notice what happened next. He cried out, and the Savior’s hand was already there. Following Jesus is not about never sinking. It is about who we call to when we do.

application.text: First, pick one thing the Savior did that you can do this week. Visit someone, forgive someone, or pray for someone. Second, when you feel doubt or fear, say Peter’s words: “Lord, save me.” Third, read one chapter in the New Testament and ask, “What does He want me to do?”

mainMessage.text: To follow Jesus Christ is to walk the way He walked. We do what He did. We love as He loved. We keep going when it is hard, and we trust Him when we cannot see far. We will not do it perfectly. But He walks ahead of us, and He lifts us when we stumble. His invitation is simple, and it is for everyone.

story.title: The rich young man

blocks.text: A young man ran to Jesus and knelt down. He wanted to know what he lacked. He had kept the commandments since he was young.

And when he was gone forth into the way, there came one running, and kneeled to him, and asked him, Good Master, what shall I do that I may inherit eternal life? And Jesus said unto him, Why callest thou me good? there is none good but one, that is, God. Thou knowest the commandments, Do not commit adultery, Do not kill, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Defraud not, Honour thy father and mother. And he answered and said unto him, Master, all these have I observed from my youth. Then Jesus beholding him loved him, and said unto him, One thing thou lackest: go thy way, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, take up the cross, and follow me. And he was sad at that saying, and went away grieved: for he had great possessions.

The scripture says Jesus loved him. The invitation came from love. The young man found it hard to let go of what he had. The scripture does not tell us what he did later. But the question stays with us. What is the one thing I find hard to give up?

application.text: First, ask the Lord in prayer, “What is one thing I lack?” Listen, and write down what comes. Second, choose one small act this week that copies something Jesus did, such as serving in secret or forgiving a hurt. Third, tell someone you trust about it so you can keep going.

I would like to talk about what it means to follow the Savior.

story.title: The fishermen leave their nets

blocks.text: Simon Peter and Andrew were working. James and John were working. It was an ordinary day. Then Jesus walked by.

And Jesus, walking by the sea of Galilee, saw two brethren, Simon called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea: for they were fishers. And he saith unto them, Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men. And they straightway left their nets, and followed him. And going on from thence, he saw other two brethren, James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, in a ship with Zebedee their father, mending their nets; and he called them. And they immediately left the ship and their father, and followed him.

The scripture says they followed straightway and immediately. They did not have the whole plan. They only had the invitation. And they said yes. Sometimes following the Savior begins on an ordinary day, with a simple yes.

application.text: First, think of one place in your life where you are trying to lead and not follow. Pray about it. Second, say yes to one invitation from the Lord this week, such as a calling, a visit, or a quiet prompting. Third, forgive yourself for last week’s missteps and try again.

So we look at His life, and we copy it as best we can.
We trust Him, even without the full map.

A child in a crowd does not need a map. She trusts the hand that holds hers. The Savior asks us to deny ourselves and take up our cross each day. That means we trust Him more than we trust our own plans. He said that whoever loses his life for His sake will find it.

And he said to them all, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me. For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: but whosoever will lose his life for my sake, the same shall save it.
Elder Richard G. Scott of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “Trust in the Lord” from the October 1995 general conference.

This life is an experience in profound trust—trust in Jesus Christ. . . . To trust means to obey willingly without knowing the end from the beginning (see Prov. 3:5–7). To produce fruit, your trust in the Lord must be more powerful and enduring than your confidence in your own personal feelings and experience.
We do not need to know the end. We need to know whose hand we are holding.
We hold on when the crowd goes the other way.

Crowds push in many directions. In the Savior’s day, a crowd of followers turned back after one hard teaching. He turned to His closest disciples and asked, “Will ye also go away?” Peter said what we can all say.

From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him. Then said Jesus unto the twelve, Will ye also go away? Then Simon Peter answered him, Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life. And we believe and are sure that thou art that Christ, the Son of the living God.
Elder Robert D. Hales of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles taught this in his talk “Christian Courage: The Price of Discipleship” from the October 2008 general conference.
Through the years we learn that challenges to our faith are not new, and they aren’t likely to disappear soon. But true disciples of Christ see opportunity in the midst of opposition.
When the crowd pulls the other way, we hold on tighter.
We grow over time.

A child grows taller each year, slowly. Following the Savior is like that. Nephi taught that after we get on the path, we keep pressing forward. We feast on the words of Christ. And the Savior told us the goal. He wants us to become like Him.

And now, my beloved brethren, after ye have gotten into this strait and narrow path, I would ask if all is done? Behold, I say unto you, Nay; for ye have not come thus far save it were by the word of Christ with unshaken faith in him, relying wholly upon the merits of him who is mighty to save. Wherefore, ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men. Wherefore, if ye shall press forward, feasting upon the word of Christ, and endure to the end, behold, thus saith the Father: Ye shall have eternal life.

And know ye that ye shall be judges of this people, according to the judgment which I shall give unto you, which shall be just. Therefore, what manner of men ought ye to be? Verily I say unto you, even as I am.
Elder D. Todd Christofferson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles wrote this in his article “To Always Remember Him” in the April 2011 Ensign. It is a magazine article, not a conference talk.

. . . I can attest that over time our desire and capacity to always remember and follow the Savior will grow. We should patiently work toward that end and pray always for the discernment and divine help we need.
Growth takes time. The Lord knows that.
He is closer than we think.
The hand in the crowd is never far away. The Lord promised to go before us. He is on our right and our left. His Spirit is in our hearts. He says, “Fear thou not; for I am with thee.”

And whoso receiveth you, there I will be also, for I will go before your face. I will be on your right hand and on your left, and my Spirit shall be in your hearts, and mine angels round about you, to bear you up.
Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness.
Elder Jeffrey R. Holland of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles taught this in his talk “Tomorrow the Lord Will Do Wonders among You” from the April 2016 general conference.

The Lord blesses those who want to improve, who accept the need for commandments and try to keep them, who cherish Christlike virtues and strive to the best of their ability to acquire them. If you stumble in that pursuit, so does everyone; the Savior is there to help you keep going. . . . Soon enough you will have the success you seek.
When we stumble, He is right there.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time about following Jesus Christ. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Zacchaeus climbs a tree

blocks.text: Zacchaeus was a rich man and a chief among the tax collectors. He wanted to see who Jesus was. But he was short, and the crowd was in the way.

And, behold, there was a man named Zacchæus, which was the chief among the publicans, and he was rich. And he sought to see Jesus who he was; and could not for the press, because he was little of stature. And he ran before, and climbed up into a sycomore tree to see him: for he was to pass that way. And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up, and saw him, and said unto him, Zacchæus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house. And he made haste, and came down, and received him joyfully.
Zacchaeus did what he could. He ran. He climbed. And the Savior stopped, looked up, and called him by name. When we do our small part to draw near to Him, He sees us. He will say our name too.

application.text: First, find your own sycamore tree. What is one thing you can do this week to get closer to Jesus? Do it. Second, make room for Him at home, in a prayer, a hymn, or a family scripture reading. Third, reach for the hand of someone who is struggling, and walk with them.

blocks.text: I know that Jesus Christ knows my name. I know that when I reach for Him, He reaches back. I know that following Him brings peace and joy. I know that He will never let go. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

closingVerse.text:
If ye keep my commandments, ye shall abide in my love; even as I have kept my Father's commandments, and abide in his love.
These things have I spoken unto you, that my joy might remain in you, and that your joy might be full.

opening.text: In the old days, a young person learned a trade by working next to a master. A carpenter’s apprentice did not start by reading a book. He stood at the bench and watched. He held the board. He made a cut, and the master showed him how to make it better. Over the years, his hands began to work like the master’s.
Jesus was a carpenter. And He invites us to be His apprentices. I would like to talk about what it means to follow Him.

mainMessage.text: To follow Jesus Christ is to learn from Him and work beside Him. He asks for our trust, our time, and our will. He asks us to stay with Him when it gets hard. He is patient with us while we learn. And He promises to stay close to us the whole way.

blocks.text: The Master asks us to come.
He did not wait for people to find Him. He found them. He said “Follow me” to Philip. His sheep hear His voice, and He knows each one. We are invited by name.
The day following Jesus would go forth into Galilee, and findeth Philip, and saith unto him, Follow me.
My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me: And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.
President Ezra Taft Benson, then President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, said this in his talk “Born of God” from the October 1985 general conference.
When you choose to follow Christ, you choose to be changed. . . . Men \[and women\] changed for Christ will be captained by Christ. . . . Their will is swallowed up in His will.
An apprentice expects to be changed. So should we.
We learn by watching Him.

An apprentice watches the master’s hands. We watch the Savior’s life. How He treated the poor. How He spoke to sinners. How He prayed. He said He had given us an example, and He asked us to do what we have seen Him do.
For I have given you an example, that ye should do as I have done to you.

Verily, verily, I say unto you, this is my gospel; and ye know the things that ye must do in my church; for the works which ye have seen me do that shall ye also do; for that which ye have seen me do even that shall ye do;
President Ezra Taft Benson said this in his article “Jesus Christ—Gifts and Expectations” in the December 1988 Ensign. It is a magazine article, not a conference talk.

That man is greatest and most blessed and joyful whose life most closely approaches the pattern of the Christ. This has nothing to do with earthly wealth, power, or prestige. The only true test of greatness, blessedness, joyfulness is how close a life can come to being like the Master, Jesus Christ. He is the right way, the full truth, and the abundant life.
The Master, Jesus Christ. Those are President Benson’s own words.
We trade our way for His.

An apprentice sets aside his own habits. He does it the master’s way, even when he does not yet see why. The Savior asks the same of us. We deny ourselves. We take up our cross daily. And in return, He says we find our lives.

And he said to them all, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me. For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: but whosoever will lose his life for my sake, the same shall save it.
Elder Richard G. Scott of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles gave this counsel in his talk “Trust in the Lord” from the October 1995 general conference.

This life is an experience in profound trust—trust in Jesus Christ. . . . To trust means to obey willingly without knowing the end from the beginning (see Prov. 3:5–7). To produce fruit, your trust in the Lord must be more powerful and enduring than your confidence in your own personal feelings and experience.
We trust that the Master knows what He is building.
We stay at the bench.

There are days when the work is hard and the lessons are slow. An apprentice may want to quit. In the Savior’s own time, many disciples left after a hard teaching. He asked the Twelve if they would leave too. Peter answered with faith.

From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him. Then said Jesus unto the twelve, Will ye also go away? Then Simon Peter answered him, Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life. And we believe and are sure that thou art that Christ, the Son of the living God.
Elder Robert D. Hales of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “Christian Courage: The Price of Discipleship” from the October 2008 general conference.
Through the years we learn that challenges to our faith are not new, and they aren’t likely to disappear soon. But true disciples of Christ see opportunity in the midst of opposition.
We stay, because we know whose words give life.
Skill comes with time.

No apprentice becomes a master in a month. It takes years. Nephi told us that entering the path is just the beginning. We press forward. We feast on the word of Christ. The Savior’s goal for us is high. He wants us to become like Him.

And now, my beloved brethren, after ye have gotten into this strait and narrow path, I would ask if all is done? Behold, I say unto you, Nay; for ye have not come thus far save it were by the word of Christ with unshaken faith in him, relying wholly upon the merits of him who is mighty to save. Wherefore, ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men. Wherefore, if ye shall press forward, feasting upon the word of Christ, and endure to the end, behold, thus saith the Father: Ye shall have eternal life.

And know ye that ye shall be judges of this people, according to the judgment which I shall give unto you, which shall be just. Therefore, what manner of men ought ye to be? Verily I say unto you, even as I am.
Elder D. Todd Christofferson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles wrote this in his article “To Always Remember Him” in the April 2011 Ensign. It is a magazine article, not a conference talk.

. . . I can attest that over time our desire and capacity to always remember and follow the Savior will grow. We should patiently work toward that end and pray always for the discernment and divine help we need.
Over time. We can be patient with that.
The Master stays beside us.
A good master does not leave the apprentice alone with the saw. He stays near. The Lord has said the same. He goes before our face. He is on our right hand and our left. His Spirit is in our hearts.

And whoso receiveth you, there I will be also, for I will go before your face. I will be on your right hand and on your left, and my Spirit shall be in your hearts, and mine angels round about you, to bear you up.
Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness.
Elder Jeffrey R. Holland of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “Tomorrow the Lord Will Do Wonders among You” from the April 2016 general conference.

The Lord blesses those who want to improve, who accept the need for commandments and try to keep them, who cherish Christlike virtues and strive to the best of their ability to acquire them. If you stumble in that pursuit, so does everyone; the Savior is there to help you keep going. . . . Soon enough you will have the success you seek.
We will make mistakes in the shop. He knows that. He helps us keep going.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time about following Jesus Christ. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Matthew leaves the tax table

blocks.text: Matthew was a tax collector. He sat at his table, doing his job. Many people did not like tax collectors. Then Jesus passed by.
And as Jesus passed forth from thence, he saw a man, named Matthew, sitting at the receipt of custom: and he saith unto him, Follow me. And he arose, and followed him.

The story is short. Jesus saw Matthew. He said two words. Matthew got up. That is all the scripture tells us. The Lord did not wait for Matthew to be ready by anyone else’s standard. He invited him as he was. And Matthew rose and followed.

application.text: First, choose one habit of the Savior to learn this month, such as praying alone, serving quietly, or forgiving fast. Practice it daily. Second, when it gets hard, return to Peter’s question: “Lord, to whom shall we go?” Third, ask someone you trust to walk with you and keep you going.

blocks.text: I know that Jesus Christ is the Master and my Savior. I know that He is patient with those who are learning. I know that He is near, even when I stumble. I know that when I follow Him, I am becoming who I am meant to be. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.
